content: The development of the guideline was meticulously overseen by a Steering Group, which included members selected from various WHO Technical Units. These units encompassed areas such as Access to Medicines and Health Products, Health Products Policy and Standards, Demographic Change and Healthy Ageing, Integrated Health Services, Mental Health and Substance Use, Gender, Equity and Human Rights, Health Promotion, Sensory Functions, Disability and Rehabilitation, Quality Health Services, and Traditional, Complementary, and Integrative Medicine. The selection of members was based on the relevance of their expertise to the work at hand. Departmental directors were asked to nominate representatives for the Steering Group, and WHO staff working in regional offices with a focus on ageing were also invited to participate. The guideline was developed following the process outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. The Steering Group played a pivotal role in supporting the creation of a guideline proposal, which was submitted to the WHO Guideline Review Committee in April 2021. The group also oversaw the selection and approval of members for the Guideline Development Group (GDG) and the External Review Group (ERG). They participated in the first GDG meeting in June 2021 and subsequently supervised the selection of suppliers for evidence syntheses. They observed the second GDG meeting in September 2022, where evidence syntheses were interpreted, and recommendations were proposed. Finally, the Steering Group reviewed and approved the draft guideline. The GDG consisted of 25 multidisciplinary clinical experts and specialists in fields such as gender, health equity, guideline methods, epidemiology, ageing, and traditional, complementary, and integrative medicine. A person with chronic low back pain (LBP) was also included to provide lived experience expertise. The ERG, comprising 14 members, was appointed to complement the GDG's skills and fill any gaps in discipline representation. The ERG included a diverse mix of clinical disciplines and technical skills, as well as a person with chronic LBP. Details of the selection process and membership profiles for both groups are provided in Web Annex A. An independent guideline methodologist was appointed to support the Technical Unit, Steering Group, and GDG in the recommendation development process. Seven systematic review teams were commissioned to evaluate the benefits and harms of prioritized interventions. These reviews included new analyses or updates to existing Cochrane or non-Cochrane reviews, assessed for quality using the AMSTAR-2 tool. The GDG participated in four virtual meeting series. The first meeting, held over three days in June 2021, focused on reaching consensus on the scope, population, priority questions, and critical outcomes. The second and third meetings, in September and December 2022, respectively, involved examining and interpreting evidence and proposing recommendations through a consensus-based approach. These meetings were facilitated by an independent methodologist and co-chaired by two GDG members. The fourth meeting, in March 2023, reviewed the draft recommendations to ensure consistency in judgments and decision criteria application. The GDG approved the final guideline document and its recommendations. Observers from global or regional organizations and governments supporting the guideline project were invited to attend the second GDG meeting as non-participating observers. Fourteen observers attended, but they did not engage in discussions or decision-making. WHO emphasized the integration of end-user perspectives into the guideline development process. A person with chronic LBP was included in both the GDG and ERG, actively contributing to formulating critical outcomes, prioritizing interventions, and developing recommendations. The GDG chairs ensured that this individual's views were considered at decision points. All external contributors were required to complete a Declaration of Interest (DOI) and Confidentiality Undertaking (CU). Observers completed only the CU. The Technical Unit reviewed all DOI forms and curricula vitae to identify potential conflicts of interest, which were managed on a case-by-case basis following WHO guidelines. Some DOIs required specific actions, such as conditional participation, partial exclusion, or total exclusion. A summary of DOI findings and their management is provided in Web Annex A. None of the declared interests were deemed serious enough to compromise the guideline development process or its credibility. The GDG identified priority questions and outcomes using the PICO format during its first meeting. Consensus decisions on critical outcomes and interventions were reached through facilitated discussions, real-time voting, and online surveys. Outcomes were ranked on a scale of 1 to 9, with those scoring 7 or higher retained as critical. Subpopulation evidence syntheses were considered for specific subgroups, such as age, gender, presence of spine-related leg pain, and race/ethnicity, where data were available. The guideline also acknowledged the social constructs and potentially offensive nature of terms used to define race and ethnicity. The guideline focused on evaluating the health and well-being benefits and harms of non-surgical interventions for managing chronic primary low back pain in community-dwelling adults, including older individuals aged 60 years and above. The interventions were compared with placebo, no intervention, or usual care. The population included adults aged 20 years and older with chronic primary low back pain, with or without co-existing spine-related leg pain. Trials with mixed populations were included if data for adults were presented separately or if the majority of participants were adults. The interventions were categorized into five classes: structured education and advice, physical interventions (active and passive), psychological interventions, medicines, and multicomponent interventions. Each intervention class was evaluated for critical outcomes such as pain, function, health-related quality of life, harms/adverse events, psychological functioning, social participation, and changes in medication use. The guideline also considered specific outcomes for older adults, such as falls and body weight. Quantitative evidence syntheses were commissioned to evaluate the benefits and harms of prioritized interventions using randomized controlled trials (RCTs). These syntheses focused on critical outcomes and adhered to the PICO criteria for evidence selection. Non-RCT research designs were not included in the evaluation process.
